prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which many laser-cooled neutral atoms are trapped at a magic wavelength, bringing atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep the optical lattice clock as a single-achievement prize with two names. Nothing in round 1 changed the physics case; the discussion mainly sharpened the answer to the chair's question about what is new. The 2005 comb prize gave a way to count optical cycles, and the 2012 prize rewarded isolating and controlling individual quantum systems, including single-ion clocks. The lattice clock is a different regime: a magic wavelength cancels the light shift of the clock transition, so a large ensemble of neutral atoms is interrogated at once. Statistical stability and systematic uncertainty then improve together, which a single ion cannot offer. That is why the field moved from the 1e-15 range to about 1e-18 and why averaging times for comparisons dropped so strongly. It is experimentally demonstrated and reproduced: independent clocks in Tokyo, Boulder, Paris, Braunschweig and elsewhere agree, with fibre-link comparisons between laboratories. It has enabled millimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurements, limits on drifts of constants, dark-matter searches and spin-squeezed clock operation. It has opened a field and enabled other work, which are the criteria I weight most. The citation I would support is tied to the magic-wavelength lattice and to demonstrated accuracy, and does not mention the redefinition of the second, which is timely but not part of the achievement. The two names also have a clear division, Katori for the proposal and the first strontium lattice clock, Ye for taking it to the accuracy and coherence frontier, which matches how the other members describe it.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 1997, 2005 and 2012 prizes remains the real risk, and I do not claim it is zero; I only argue that the ensemble magic-wavelength step is not covered by any of them. Danielsson's point that a clock is a measurement method and not a discovery about nature is also not fully answered: no new physics has been seen with these clocks, and the constants and geodesy payoffs are still partly prospective. Nobody here, including me, has checked the priority history of the magic-wavelength proposal and the first lattice clocks against primary papers, and Lemonde and the Paris group, Boulder and NIST contributors and the ion-clock community have genuine claims that two names compress. Finally, I am a Boulder-adjacent member judging an AMO result, so my familiarity could inflate my confidence, which is a reason to weigh my statement alongside Lindroth's and Johansson's and not above them.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to B042 for robustness, citing the prediction-then-measurement chain, independent confirmation in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and ARPES, and a clean theory-plus-experiment structure, and asked the AMO members whether Katori and Ye are separable from Hall, Hansch and Wineland.
responses.response: I take the robustness argument seriously and I rate B042 as a mature, reproduced field, which is why it is my first alternative. On his question: the comb prize concerned the tool that counts optical cycles and the 2012 prize concerned control of individual quantum systems; neither covers trapping an ensemble at a magic wavelength so that stability and accuracy improve together. That is separable. On B042 itself, my earlier concern about Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang has not been answered in round 1. Eriksson, Mehlig and Olsson all agree that BHZ pointed Molenkamp to HgTe and that Zhang's death makes the record uneven, and a Kane, Mele, Molenkamp citation then credits the experiment and half of the theory that it tested. If a citation could be worded as the Z2 prediction and its observation, without implying the whole chain, I would not oppose it; I just do not rank it above a credit that has no comparable hole.

responses.point: Mehlig moved to B042 as a simple, general mechanism confirmed by nature, but states that if the committee cannot accept the omissions, B037 with its clean two-person credit is the better choice and he would not stand in its way.
responses.response: I read this as a real convergence on method: we both want a prize resting on a result nature could have refused and that several laboratories reproduced. I accept his criterion and I think B037 meets it, since an ensemble clock at 1e-18 is a quantitative test that is passed by independent intercomparisons, not by one group. I also accept his earlier objection to my own case: much of the value is the engineering of systematic uncertainty, and the fundamental result is prospective. I answer that the engineering is the discovery here, because showing that a lattice-induced shift can be cancelled and that blackbody and other shifts can be controlled to 1e-18 is a measured property of nature that was not known to be reachable. I also note that his stated fallback and my first alternative point to each other, so the committee is not split on science, only on how much weight to give attribution risk.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers the ATLAS and CMS Higgs discovery as a discovery about what the world is made of, calls the three-name leadership credit a compromise, and says he would not block B037 if the committee cannot defend it.
responses.response: I agree with him that the discovery is mature and important, and I do not dispute that the 2013 prize left the experimental half unrewarded. My difficulty is the one he names: the three credited people are founding spokespersons and project leaders, and Olsson points out that the spokespersons at the time of discovery were others. I cannot judge from this record who made the decisive contribution, and a prize that honours leadership would need a public rationale the statutes can bear. On his distinction between a discovery and a method, I think it is real but not decisive: the statute speaks of a discovery or an invention, and the clock is an invention with published figures of merit. I note his willingness to accept B037 as a fallback and I would ask the chair to record that, since it removes the main obstacle to a decision.

responses.point: Olsson moved from B012 to B042, arguing that Mele must be credited to avoid a gap in the theory half, that Xue's quantum anomalous Hall experiment is a separate loss, and that the 2016 prize covered a different lineage than time-reversal-invariant Z2 insulators.
responses.response: I find her distinction between the 2016 Thouless, Haldane, Kosterlitz lineage and Z2 band topology persuasive, so I no longer count the 2016 prize as a strong objection to B042, which is a change from my first-round position. I also agree that Kane and Mele together plus Molenkamp is the best mapping of the supplied names. My remaining doubt is whether any three names can carry the story once Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D work are set aside, whereas B037 needs no such compromise. I would therefore order B037 first and B042 second, and I would change that order if the AMO review of priority history turned up a serious problem with the Katori and Ye split.

responses.point: Johansson moved her first choice from circuit QED to B037, partly because of her proximity to the circuit-QED community, and wants a citation built on the magic-wavelength lattice that says what is new relative to ion clocks.
responses.response: I agree with her reasoning and welcome the change, and I note that it was made in spite of a proximity that would have favoured B008. I accept her wording request: my round-2 citation is explicitly about trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, and it is silent about the second. I also agree with her flag about Girvin and Huang on B008, which is why I keep it only as a second alternative and not as a serious competitor, together with the timing problem after the 2025 prize. Because of my own WACQT role I should not be an influential voice on circuit QED, so I give it no more weight than that.

uncertainties: The priority history of Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium lattice clock against the contemporaneous Ye, Paris and Boulder work has still not been checked against primary papers by anyone in this room; Lindroth recalls it from memory and I have not verified it. I would want an expert note before the final ballot.
Whether the committee accepts that the ensemble magic-wavelength lattice is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or sees it as evolutionary.

Whether two names are enough given the claims of Lemonde and the Paris group, other JILA and NIST contributors and the ion-clock groups; I see no clear third name in the supplied record and padding would weaken the citation.
How the still-pending redefinition of the second should count for timing, which I think it should not in the citation.
Whether a satisfactory Kane, Mele, Molenkamp wording exists that answers the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang omission; this is the one thing that could move B042 above B037 for me.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1, restated for the record. During my PhD I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye is a scientific descendant of that JILA environment; I have no personal, financial or collaborative tie to Ye or Katori, but the committee may judge whether a recusal question arises for B037. If the committee thinks it does, I will abstain from the final ballot on that part. Separately, my executive role at the Chalmers-led Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology overlaps institutionally with Johansson and with the superconducting-circuit field behind B008, so I should not decide on circuit QED. I am also on the management team of Deep Light Vision, which has no connection to any shortlisted candidate.
